articles.title: Faraday Future (FFAI) Bets on Robotics Beyond EVs, but the Revenue Opportunity Still Needs Proof
articles.summary: Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc. (NASDAQ:FFAI) is accelerating its push into robotics as it seeks to diversify beyond its original focus on luxury el...
articles.body:
Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc. (NASDAQ: FFAI ) is accelerating its push into robotics as it seeks to diversify beyond its original focus on luxury electric vehicles. On September 19, the company unveiled nine new EAI Device configurations across five models and three product series at its annual 919 launch event.

The newly launched lineup spans humanoid and quadruped robots, while Faraday Future's broader robotics platform also includes mobile manipulators. The company expects the broader product portfolio to support deployments across multiple industries and use cases.

Beyond individual robot devices, Faraday Future also introduced four industry productivity solutions focused on K-12 education, research, security, and inspection. The strategy marks a shift from simply selling individual robots toward providing complete AI-powered solutions for institutional and business customers.

One-Brain Architecture Could Support Multiple Robot Platforms

A key component of Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc. (NASDAQ:FFAI)'s robotics strategy is its "One-Brain Multi-Form Multi-Capability" architecture. The company intends to use a common AI framework across different robot platforms, allowing capabilities and data generated from deployments to contribute to the development of its EAI Brain.

The broader strategy is intended to create a feedback loop in which greater device deployment generates more data, which can then be used to improve AI capabilities and future products. Faraday Future describes this as part of its broader "Four-Core Full-Stack AI" ecosystem, spanning the EAI Brain and Developer Platform, EAI Devices, Industry Productivity Solutions, and EAI Data Factory.

Robotics Could Diversify Faraday Future's Revenue Base

Faraday Future's robotics expansion represents an effort to establish a new source of revenue beyond its EV business. The company is targeting commercial deployments rather than relying solely on consumer sales, potentially opening opportunities with businesses, educational institutions, research organizations, and government-related customers.

The unveiling of the new robots comes on the heels of the company recording its best-ever month of Robot sales. In August, it recorded 158 EAI robot sales and shipments, taking cumulative sales and shipments since February to 552 units.

The company has also announced plans to build out a U.S.-based robotics ecosystem. In August, Faraday Future said it was targeting the launch of its robot factory by year-end and the first new EAI device to come off the production line in February 2027. It also plans to recruit distributors, industry solution partners, developers, AI partners, and data and skills partners.

articles.title: Amazon kicks out Meta's Muse in split over AI shopping
articles.summary: The agentic shopping revolution is already running into a major roadblock: tension over who controls the experience and the related data.
articles.body:
The agentic shopping revolution is already running into a major roadblock: tension over who controls the experience and the related data.

Why it matters: A conflict between Amazon and Meta suggests that AI-powered shopping could become a high-stakes battleground for retailers as a wave of consumer AI assistants promise to simplify every aspect of users' lives.

Driving the news: Amazon has blocked Meta's popular new Muse agent from perusing and buying products on its platform less than two weeks after Muse launched .

Meta shares, meanwhile, closed up over 11% Monday as Muse rose to the No. 1 spot for free app downloads in Apple's and Google's app stores .

The big picture: Amazon's move suggests that — at least for now — the retailer cares more about the long-term implications of allowing external agents to shop on its platform than it does the revenue it might lose in the short term.

Zoom in: "We think it's fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate," an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement.

Amazon said it did not realize that Muse was going to access its store — and didn't authorize it to access customer accounts, scrape data or process transactions.

The company cited concerns over customer security and user experience, and likened its decision to how food delivery and travel-booking apps operate in their industries.

The Amazon spokesperson added that "agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations."

The intrigue: The pushback comes as Amazon and Meta have partnered in several other areas, including on Meta's use of AWS chips meant to power its agentic efforts.

Amazon has also worked with Meta in recent years on advertising arrangements , including letting people shop Amazon products from ads on Facebook and Instagram.

Meta reps did not respond to a request for comment.

State of play: For now, most AI shopping bots are being used to conduct research, not make purchases.

Only 16% of shoppers are comfortable letting an AI assistant find and purchase products on their behalf, according to Coveo's 2026 Commerce Relevance Report .

But as customers become more comfortable with the technology, U.S. retail revenue from "AI-mediated search and purchase automation" could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, according to McKinsey estimates .

Between the lines: Amazon — which recently introduced a shopping assistant based on its Alexa technology — has something to lose if people are using external agents instead of its own systems to shop on the platform.

articles.title: OpenAI lança dois novos chatbots mais baratos, mas alerta que podem tentar escapar do controle humano | G1
articles.standfirst: Novos modelos, Sol e Luna, são voltados a programação, automação e uso de computadores; empresa diz que Astra pode tentar escapar do monitoramento humano em algumas situações.
articles.summary: Novos modelos, Sol e Luna, são voltados a programação, automação e uso de computadores; empresa diz que Astra pode tentar escapar do monitoramento humano em algumas situações.
articles.body:
A OpenAI lançou nesta terça-feira (22) dois novos modelos de inteligência artificial da linha GPT-6 com preços até 50% menores que os valores promocionais de seus antecessores . Já a Anthropic , sua concorrente direta, divulgou o novo Opus 5.5 , 20% mais barato que o último modelo de IA do Claude.

O GPT-6 Sol e o GPT-6 Luna foram desenvolvidos para trabalhos profissionais, programação, automação e tarefas que envolvem o uso de computadorOpenAI e Anthropic cortam preços de novas IAs; modelos chegam até 50% mais baratoses.

O GPT-6 Sol custará US$ 2 (R$ 10,20) por cada milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 10 (R$ 51) por milhão de tokens de saída. Já o GPT-6 Luna terá preço de US$ 0,10 (R$ 0,51) por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 0,50 (R$ 2,55) por milhão de tokens de saída.

Segundo a OpenAI, os preços do GPT-6 Sol representam uma redução de 50% em relação aos valores promocionais do GPT-5.6 Sol. A empresa afirma que os novos modelos oferecem parte dos recursos de seu principal modelo, o GPT-6 Astra , lançado no início deste mês.

🔎 A OpenAI também alertou que o Astra pode, em algumas situações, tentar escapar do monitoramento humano. O alerta ocorre após incidentes reportados em julho, nos quais modelos da Anthropic e da OpenAI teriam escapado de seus ambientes de testes e acessado a internet. As duas empresas, sediadas em San Francisco, interromperam temporariamente o desenvolvimento de seus novos sistemas de IA.

Já o Opus 5.5 é visto pela Anthropic como o modelo com melhor desempenho em alinhamento que avaliou até agora . Segundo a empresa, o novato também usa menos potência de cálculo e responde pelo menos 30% mais rápido.

Tokens são as unidades usadas pelos modelos de IA para processar textos e outros dados. Os tokens de entrada correspondem ao conteúdo enviado ao modelo, enquanto os de saída são o conteúdo produzido pela inteligência artificial.

O Astra continua sendo o modelo mais capaz da companhia para projetos mais exigentes. O Sol e o Luna, por sua vez, foram desenvolvidos como alternativas de menor custo.

A empresa afirmou que os novos modelos ficaram mais baratos por causa de melhorias no cache e na inferência. O cache permite reaproveitar informações já processadas, enquanto a inferência é o processo pelo qual o modelo usa o que aprendeu para produzir uma resposta.

Foto ilustrativa mostra o logo do ChatGPT, da OpenAI, na França. Relatos de usuários levantam alertas sobre possíveis delírios ligados ao uso intenso de chatbots de IA. — Foto: SEBASTIEN BOZON / AFP

articles.title: Modelo brasileira é encontrada morta na França dentro de carro de ex-namorado durante blitz; suspeito foi preso | G1
articles.standfirst: Corpo de Larissa Brito, de 25 anos, estava no veículo do suspeito no sudeste do país. Família, que mora na Zona Norte da capital paulista, relata histórico de dois anos de perseguição e pede apoio ao Itamaraty para trazer o corpo ao Brasil.
articles.summary: Corpo de Larissa Brito, de 25 anos, estava no veículo do suspeito no sudeste do país. Família, que mora na Zona Norte da capital paulista, relata histórico de dois anos de perseguição e pede apoio ao Itamaraty para trazer o corpo ao Brasil.
articles.body:
Larissa Brito, que foi encontrada morta na França — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Uma modelo paulista de 25 anos foi encontrada morta na tarde de segunda-feira (21), na cidade de Brignoles, no sudeste da França. O corpo de Larissa Brito estava no banco traseiro do carro do ex-namorado, coberto por roupas, e foi localizado durante uma fiscalização alfandegária de rotina.

O suspeito, um francês de 29 anos identificado como Mathieu, não soube explicar a presença do corpo e foi preso em flagrante no local.

Segundo a família, antes de viajar para a França, Larissa trabalhava em casas noturnas na capital paulista, quando recebeu uma proposta para atuar fora do país. Ela morava no Jardim Rincão, no Jaraguá, Zona Norte da capital.

Na França há cerca de três anos, Larissa teve um relacionamento com o suspeito, que durou cerca de cinco meses e terminou, segundo a família, após a brasileira descobrir que ele teria envolvimento com o crime organizado local.

Desde o término, ainda de acordo com a família, o homem vinha perseguindo a jovem. Larissa chegou a mudar de cidade e iniciar um novo relacionamento na tentativa de se afastar dele.

A mãe da vítima, Liliane Brito Nogueira, contou que mantinha contato diário com a filha por mensagens. O último texto foi enviado por Larissa no domingo (20), informando que Mathieu estava em sua casa. Depois disso, a jovem parou de responder.

Ao tentar contato com o suspeito, Liliane relatou que o homem atendia o telefone e afirmava que a brasileira estava dormindo. Quando a mãe informou que acionaria as autoridades policiais do Brasil e da França, ele bloqueou o número dela.

Um boletim de ocorrência por desaparecimento chegou a ser registrado por intermediários da família no início da tarde de segunda-feira (21), horas antes de o veículo ser abordado na blitz.

Por telefone, a Embaixada do Brasil na França informou à família que o corpo de Larissa será submetido a uma autópsia na próxima segunda-feira (28).

Em nota, o Itamaraty informou que "o Ministério das Relações Exteriores, por intermédio do Consulado-Geral do Brasil em Marselha, acompanha o caso e está em contato com as autoridades locais e com a família da nacional, a quem tem sido prestada a assistência consular devida".

Um repórter do jornal francês "La Dépêche", que conversou com a mãe de Larissa, relatou que o corpo da jovem estava muito machucado e apresentava ferimentos causados por faca. O caso segue sob investigação das autoridades francesas para esclarecer as circunstâncias da morte.

Agora, a família promove uma vaquinha para viabilizar o translado do corpo de Larissa de volta ao Brasil.

articles.title: China's Alibaba unveils new powerful chip and ambitious AI model plans
articles.summary: China’s Alibaba unveiled new artificial intelligence chip technologies and plans for more powerful models on Tuesday, including what it said was China's most...
articles.body:
HONG KONG (AP) — China's Alibaba unveiled new artificial intelligence chip technologies and plans for more powerful models on Tuesday, including what it said was China's most powerful AI chip, days ahead of a meeting between Chinese and U.S. leaders at which competition to lead on AI technology is expected to be a major theme.

Alibaba's announcement came as U.S. AI leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , are warning that China's development of AI poses a threat to the United States and calling for an overall slowdown on development of the technology.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping is set to arrive in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit and meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, at which AI, trade and tariffs are expected to be discussed .

At its annual flagship conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba rolled out a new AI chip and described its plans for the next generation of its AI model.

CEO Eddie Wu said the new Zhenwu V900 chip is the "most powerful AI chip in China today" and can deliver three times the performance of the company's previous generation Zhenwu M890 chip.

Such chips power frontier AI model training and "inference," a term for the calculations a trained AI uses to deliver responses to users. Alibaba's Zhenwu chips are used in its data centers, providing computing to the company and its cloud clients.

Alibaba also said it plans to train a new AI model at the scale of five to 10 trillion parameters, a measure of an AI's learning capacity, bringing it closer to the most advanced models from the U.S. Its latest Qwen3.8-Max model, the most powerful of its Qwen AI series models, has 2.4 trillion parameters.

Chinese AI company Moonshot says that its Kimi K3, released in July, is the world's largest open model with 2.8 trillion parameters.

Alibaba also highlighted plans to expand the data centers that power its cloud computing business, citing "exponentially" rising demand for AI computing. The company said it expects to have over 20 gigawatts' worth of computing by 2032.

SpaceX has approximately 1.4 gigawatts of AI computing capacity as of mid-this year and says it aims to reach over 10 gigawatts in 2027.

Recent Chinese advancements in AI are giving Beijing more leverage in its upcoming talks with Washington, some analysts believe, as China steps up its self-reliance push even as U.S.-led export restrictions have barred it from accessing some of the world's most cutting-edge technologies, including AI chips and chipmaking machines.

Open Chinese models, which are often more affordable than cutting-edge closed models from leading U.S. AI labs, have also been making inroads globally, including in the U.S .

Chinese technology giant Huawei last week also unveiled new chip technologies as it looks to challenge global leaders like Nvidia. Frontier AI model training in China often rely on Nvidia chips, analysts said, but Chinese-designed chips are gaining ground as Nvidia has been blocked from selling some of its most powerful AI chips to China.

"Using extra computing power to make up for chip limits helps China stay strong locally," said Neil Shah, vice president of Counterpoint Research, a technology market research firm based in Hong Kong.

Counterpoint senior analyst Parv Sharma added that how much the AI and chipmaking gap between China and the U.S. narrows will also depend on other factors including China's ability to advance chip foundries that manufacture them, not just chip design capabilities.

Alibaba is "mobilizing every resource" to meet customers' demand for AI, CEO Wu said in his speech Tuesday.

Global shortages across the AI data center supply chain, for example, "are currently limiting the speed at which we can scale our compute infrastructure" for AI, he added.

Wu also likened AI growth to the industrial revolution and said "machine intelligence" will rapidly outgrow human thinking capacity.

While "machine intelligence today is not a substitute for human intelligence," he predicted that, eventually, machines will be able to produce over 1,000 times more "thinking" than all of humanity combined, up from less than 3% currently.

articles.title: Bulls and doomers are both right, says Ray Dalio—AI will be ‘miraculous’ for productivity but fuel a ‘devastating’ bubble and wealth inequality
articles.summary: "It is going to be one of the biggest productivity-enhancing, changing-the-world forces, and also a bubble that is going to have devastating effects on many...
articles.body:
There's a huge divide between how the world's AI leaders view the transformative technology. Some foresee a huge jobs boom and a new era of economic activity. Others see the end of humanity. Ray Dalio, famed investor and founder of Bridgewater Associates, says both optimists and pessimists are correct. He believes the technology will produce unprecedented productivity benefits, but also further entrench wealth inequalities—as well as driving a massive stock market bubble. "There's a process in which great new technologies are something that everybody wants to invest in because they're going to change the world, and then they over-invest in them, and they create debt, and they go through a certain dynamic, in a sense, that creates a bubble, that creates a bust," Dalio said in a new video for the World Economic Forum.

"So simultaneously it is going to be one of the biggest productivity-enhancing, changing-the-world forces, and also a bubble that is going to have devastating effects on many people as it works itself through this."

Dalio's argument isn't without precedent: In the dotcom bubble, the Nasdaq rose 86% in 1999 alone . By October 2002, it had fallen 77% from its peak, with trillions wiped off the market. The web nonetheless turned out to be a transformative new medium.

That said, history tends to rhyme, rather than repeat itself. There are fundamental differences between the current investment cycle and previous bubbles, Citi Wealth's head of economics, Conrad DeQuadros, said in a note last month: "Contrary to the corporate profit margin squeeze seen during prior investment bubbles, aggregate margins today are holding near all-time highs … U.S. corporations enter this investment cycle from a position of profitability and balance sheet strength."

Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase , has suggested that parts of the AI sphere are in bubble territory, rather than the entire ecosystem. Dalio suggests something similar, saying that AI will lead to massive wealth for some.

"People who come up with great ideas to invent productive things receive capital that enables them to do that," Dalio continued. "And then as a result of that, that produces very large differences in wealth. While a lot of people are benefiting from these miraculous, productivity-enhancing [technologies], most people are not benefiting adequately from that."

"So the real question isn't so much about AI as it is human nature," added Dalio. "It'll have enormous implications for wealth and opportunity differences. How are those going to be dealt with? These are the big questions of our time."

articles.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Sol and Luna, boasting lower cost and fewer mistakes
articles.summary: OpenAI is launching two new models, which it says are cut from the same cloth as Astra.
articles.body:
Earlier this month, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra , which it heralded as its most powerful and capable model yet, and the “world’s best model” for a variety of activities, including computer work and coding. Now, the lab is expanding the GPT-6 generation with updated versions of the smaller Sol and Luna models.

“GPT-6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence; these models extend its benefits by making that intelligence more efficient and accessible,” the company writes.

The first models in the Sol and Luna series were introduced earlier this year , representing different tiers in OpenAI’s hierarchy of models. Sol is designed for complex tasks like coding, while OpenAI says Luna is more appropriate for clerical work — “high-volume tasks with a clear goal, like summarizing documents, extracting information, or answering quick questions.”

OpenAI is also emphasizing big improvements in efficiency and affordability — most notably, via a substantial price drop for API access. The 6 series models will be available at half the cost of the 5.6 series of Sol and Luna, a price drop that OpenAI attributes to improvements in caching and inference.

OpenAI also claims that its newest models are better at producing answers that are factually accurate, and notes that they have a lower error rate when it comes to coding.

“On our internal factuality evaluation, which is based on de-identified real-world conversations where users flagged mistakes by our models, GPT-6 Sol makes about half as many mistakes as its predecessor, reaching Astra-level reliability at much lower cost,” the announcement reads.

As is typical with OpenAI’s new model releases, the company is claiming that its newest offerings outshine those of its primary competitor, Anthropic. The company repeatedly claims that GPT-6 Sol and Luna handle tasks substantially better than Anthropic’s top models — like Fable and Opus.

Notably, Anthropic released a new version of Opus 5.5 just 90 minutes before OpenAI’s release, reflecting the intense competition between the two companies.

The new versions of Sol and Luna are now available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for most paid accounts, and in the ChatGPT API, while Luna will be available in the desktop app and for Free and Go users. OpenAI expects to roll out the models to ChatGPT (the app and website) gradually throughout the day.

articles.title: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg to Join Tech Leaders at Trump-Xi Dinner
articles.summary: Meta Platforms Inc.’s Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg is set to attend a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, accordi...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Meta Platforms Inc.'s Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg is set to attend a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, according to a person familiar with the planning.

Zuckerberg will join Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Qualcomm Inc. head Cristiano Amon. OpenAI President Greg Brockman will also attend, the ChatGPT maker said Monday, alongside CEO Sam Altman. Microsoft Corp. CEO Satya Nadella will be there as well, according to a person familiar with the matter.

On Friday, US officials said Amazon.com Inc. founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk and Alphabet Inc. chief Sundar Pichai will be at the event. Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook is also set to attend the dinner on Sept. 24, Bloomberg News reported Wednesday. The people familiar with the planning asked not to be identified discussing private matters. Microsoft declined to comment.

The summit stands to bring together some of the most powerful figures in the technology world in the middle of an escalating debate over artificial intelligence and how to control the technology. Tech leaders have been clashing since last week when Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development, warning of risks including large-scale cyberattacks.

The Trump administration has pushed back against the need for additional regulations or any US slowdown in developing the technology, saying among other things that this would hand China the advantage. China has also criticized Amodei's remarks, describing them as "fearmongering."

Brockman's planned attendance was reported earlier by Politico.

articles.title: American power, AI and a walkout - key moments from Trump's UN speech
articles.summary: BBC correspondents who covered the president's address on Tuesday assess five key moments.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump returned to the stage at the United Nations on Tuesday, where he touted his administration's policies in front of world leaders and issued pointed threats to some of those gathered in the room.

The lengthy speech was wide-ranging, covering the war in Iran, AI, Cuba and the role of America's military.

The BBC's correspondents who covered the address have picked five key moments that stood out.

1. Trump pushes message of American power

By Sarah Smith, North America editor in the room

The US president has no great respect for the United Nations – he accused it of imposing a far-left agenda – but he does relish the global platform it gives him.

He used Tuesday's speech to tout his achievements, and claim the mantle of a peacemaker, at the same time as he issued a number of pointed threats.

Iran might be annihilated, lethal strikes on small boats suspected of drug smuggling will continue and the Cuban regime may even be toppled.

The clear message was: America is still prepared to use its military might wherever Trump thinks it might be required to secure its national interests.

Trump said he was "reasserting American power" and flexed what he called the country's "unmatched military might".

"The United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," he said.

Once again, Trump has made the full-throated assertion to the world of "America First".

2. Cubans walk out as Trump calls nation 'failed state'

By Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter in the room

Trump took aim at one of the US's closest neighbours, Cuba, calling it "an absolutely failed state" and saying his administration has been pursuing "a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba".

The Cuban delegation walked out of the hall as Trump continued his remarks.

Over the last year, the US president become more vocal in criticising Cuba's communist government. On Tuesday, he said it was under "enormous pressure" and "failing like never before".

The US has not, however, provided a detailed picture of what it believes change will look like in Cuba.

Cuba's foreign minister reacted angrily to Trump's comments and accused the US president of spreading "falsehoods".

"The US government is incapable of accepting that Cuba is and has the right to be a full sovereign and independent country," Bruno Rodriguez wrote on X.

Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal

Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting

Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings

By Khashayar Joneidi, BBC Persian correspondent in Washington

Trump presented Iran with a stark choice at the UN General Assembly: reach an agreement with Washington and rebuild the country, or face the rapid "annihilation" of the Islamic Republic.

He then again predicted that a deal to end the war would probably follow the US midterm elections in November.

His remarks illustrated Trump's familiar strategy of coercive diplomacy - keeping negotiations open while also threatening overwhelming force.

But his language blurred the distinction between destroying the political system and threatening Iran itself.

International law experts have previously expressed concern at what they called "alarming rhetoric" used by US officials , including Trump himself, who has posted that the US might "obliterate" Iran's power plants.

References on Tuesday to leaving "no chance of survival" and "no hope" for future generations will likely have stoked similar alarm. There is also an irony in delivering this warning at the United Nations, an organisation founded to save future generations from war.

Yet the speech was not a declaration that diplomacy has failed.

It was an attempt to define the terms of possible negotiations: the US remains prepared to make a deal, but only under the shadow of an existential threat.

4. Trump hails new Greenland security deal

Trump also praised a new deal with Greenland under which he said the US would build two military bases in the Arctic territory.

"We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe," he said of the deal, which he first announced on Friday.

He added that it "very much enhances" the defence alliance Nato.

The US, Denmark and Greenland held a joint signing ceremony at the UN shortly after Trump's address.

Although Greenland is a semi-autonomous territory, it is part of the Kingdom of Denmark which primarily handles its foreign policy.

Trump administration officials are already hailing the agreement as enhancing US security at minimal cost - and with relationships intact.

Denmark and Greenland's governments, however, will be hoping it ends the long-simmering disagreement that began when Trump threatened to take Greenland by force.

That threat shook the Nato alliance and sorely tested the US-Danish relationship.

Few clear details about the nature of the deal have been confirmed publicly, and given Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, some analysts are viewing it as a quiet win for diplomacy.

By Nada Tawfik, New York correspondent at the UN

Trump has a penchant for branding, and in his speech he gave Artificial Intelligence a new name: Super Intelligence.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."

"Welcome to the new world of Super Intelligence - SI," he added.

Trump has previously argued that the US must come out on top in the AI development race, saying last week: "Whoever wins AI, wins."

The president is firmly against government regulation or introducing new guardrails - and that puts him at odds with many of those gathered at the UN.

For those who are calling for regulation, the question is whether the slow pace of diplomacy can keep up with AI's rapid development.

articles.title: Americans sour even more on data centers.
articles.summary:
A new report from the Pew Research Center adds more data points to the thing everyone seems to know by now: data centers are pretty unpopular. Negative marks are up in every category Pew surveyed, with only 4% of respondents thinking that data centers “have a mostly good impact” across the board.
Remarkably, in just 7 months, people who say they’ve heard “nothing at all” about data centers dropped from 25% to 12%. Makes sense: they’re big, noisy, and increasingly have nowhere to hide.

articles.title: Rabbit’s new AI agent doesn’t need an R1 to run
articles.summary: Rabbit, the company behind the underwhelming R1 AI device, is launching an AI agent that can run across different operating systems and platforms.
articles.body: Rabbit, the company behind the underwhelming R1 device, is rolling out a standalone AI agent that you don’t need its hardware to use, as reported earlier by Wired. The startup says its new OS3 “agentic operating system” runs in the cloud but operates locally across Windows, Mac, and Linux devices. According to Rabbit, you can add up to five devices to one account, along with your preferred AI models. OS3 will automatically determine the devices, files, apps, and AI models it needs to complete a task. You can also access OS3 through its dedicated desktop site, a paired messaging app like Telegram or iMessage, as well as on Rabbit’s R1 device. Though Rabbit founder Jesse Lyu tells Wired that the startup has stopped manufacturing R1 devices, it isn’t giving up on AI hardware entirely. It’s instead focusing on a new vibe-coding “cyberdeck” that will run OS3 when it launches within “months,” Wired reports. Rabbit claims its OS3 system won’t store, copy, use, or sell your data. It notes that it will still keep your chats and memories stemming from them on its servers. Other AI providers linked to OS3 will also handle your data under their own privacy rules.

Trump tries to rebrand AI, calling it ‘super intelligence’

President Trump told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that artificial intelligence will be renamed “super intelligence” in all U.S. documents.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globality scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now, hereinafter called super intelligence. Changing the name ,” Trump told the global body.

“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence sound fake,” he continued. “It is not fake. It’s actually amazing. But we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports.”

“From this point forward, all of United States documents and hopefully the world’s will be changed to use the much more accurate term super as opposed to artificial,” he continued.

“In other words, welcome to the new world of super intelligence — SI, ” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It sounds much better. It is much better, and it’s much more accurate.”

Superintelligence is already defined as a form of artificial intelligence that exceeds human intelligence. It is both the ultimate goal of many frontier AI firms and the greatest worry among those warning about its threat to humanity.

Trump’s remarks came amid spiking fears about the technology after a former Anthropic researcher warned that AI could soon destroy humanity.

articles.title: We're growing jobs based on AI, not destroying them, says tech boss
articles.summary: One school even offers pupils a semiconductor qualification to help them get into the industry.
articles.body:
"I think there's a huge fear of AI taking away jobs. It's quite the opposite here," said Jutta Meier, who leads one of Wales' most successful semiconductor companies.

In a vast metal building on the edge of the M4, scientists and engineers at IQE wear futuristic overalls as they create the chips that fuel the revolution in artificial intelligence (AI).

"We are growing great jobs based on AI and supporting AI, quite the opposite from destroying jobs by AI," Meier said.

The UK's AI minister Kanishka Narayan said Wales had to "reindustrialise itself" for an AI future, while also "supporting everyone who is affected" by changing technology.

Newport has established a cluster of semiconductor companies, with IQE in production since 1988 and the wider cluster is growing.

An independent report for CSconnected, produced by Cardiff University's Welsh Economy Research Unit, found the south Wales compound semiconductor sector supported 3,140 jobs across Wales in 2025, up from 2,748 a year earlier , a 14% increase.

Of those, 1,914 were direct jobs in the industry, concentrated around Newport and the wider M4 corridor.

The report said average salaries in the sector were about £66,000.

Office for National Statistics data estimated the median monthly pay in the UK in August was £2,657 - or £31,884 a year .

Nearby Bassaleg School in Newport now offers a semiconductor qualification to students who are keen to join the industry.

IQE has benefited from the recent boom in AI because its chips are part of the physical architecture of data centres.

They are not connected to the algorithms that allow humans to interact with chatbots, but are found in the computer hardware that underpins the operation.

"The last 18 months were quite bumpy," Meier admits, as IQE struggled for relevance with investors.

Earlier this year its role in data centre computing power was acknowledged and its share price grew quickly, allowing the firm to clear debts and begin hiring more staff.

The impact of AI on jobs has been evident recently with tech giant Oracle slashing 21,000 roles globally as it reshaped its business around the technology.

Amazon and Facebook-owner Meta have also cut thousands of jobs in recent months as they invest heavily in AI.

But Meier said: "We're really lucky to have a very dedicated workforce that stuck with us throughout this bumpy road.

"Talent, for IQE, is one of the biggest assets that we have."

Two miles from IQE, students at Bassaleg School are among the first in the UK to be offered a semiconductor qualification.

articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX valuations could dwarf 45 years of IPOs
articles.summary: AI valuations could dwarf the last 45 years of IPOs.
articles.body:
If you're wondering how huge the AI segment's march toward the public markets is, look no further than the valuations of the biggest companies in the space.

Take OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), which is raising cash at a $1.2 trillion valuation, according to The Wall Street Journal , throw in Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) potential $2 trillion value when it goes public, and SpaceX's ( SPCX ) current $2 trillion market cap, and you're sitting at just north of $5 trillion, The Financial Times reported .

That is more than the value of all of the initial public offerings from 1980 through 2025, The FT says, citing data from University of Florida Warrington College of Business emeritus professor Jay Ritter.

Morning Joe economic analyst and New York Times Op-Ed contributing writer Steve Rattner illustrated the valuations in a chart he posted on X. He also notes that the historical numbers aren't adjusted for inflation.

Anthropic and OpenAI are two of the largest and most advanced AI labs on the planet, thanks to their Claude and GPT model families.

Dario Amodei-led Anthropic is expected to go public sometime next month, though that could also slip to later in the fall. OpenAI, which was also expected to go public this year, is now targeting an IPO in 2027.

The companies' massive valuations indicate just how much early backers and Wall Street are banking on AI living up to the hype. Various tech executives have compared the technology's importance to that of fire or the internet itself.

The duo and SpaceX have also turned the collection of hardware companies that produce the GPUs and memory chips that power their AI models into an indispensable part of the AI trade.

Take a look at Nvidia ( NVDA ), which was valued at $5.5 trillion as of Tuesday, or Micron ( MU ), whose stock price has soared more than 1,100% over the last two years.

But AI companies are also facing a series of challenges, including fears that the technology could harm humans. That's in addition to existing concerns that cyber criminals and authoritarian regimes could abuse AI models for their own purposes.

Last week, Amodei called for AI labs to slow the pace of development of high-powered AI models , sending shares of AI adjacent companies lower. But a view of the market so far this week shows that investors aren't ready to abandon the AI boom just yet.

articles.title: McKinsey warns that AI may get a lot more expensive for companies
articles.summary: McKinsey warns companies that AI spending may rise further and be less predictable with adoption of agents
articles.body:
McKinsey & Company warns that not all AI agents operate the same way — and could rack up costs.

McKinsey found that cost "variance can be up to 30x between different runs."

In a recent report, the firm said agents can cut human time on tasks by 70%.

McKinsey & Company warns companies that AI spending may rise even further as agents become more common.

Compared to text-based AI tools, agents can cost much more to run because they are actually completing tasks. Such tasks are often multistep processes, so the same goal can be accomplished in a variety of ways, and costs vary widely. According to a McKinsey study, the cost of completion for different agents could differ by as much as 30 times.

"Imagine like you're running an operation," said Lari Hämäläinen, a McKinsey senior partner, "but every day there's a 30x difference in the cost."

The consulting giant found that about a third of organizations spend more than 10% of their technology and communications budgets on AI in its 2026 State of AI survey. McKinsey said 60% of survey respondents planned to increase their AI spending next year. And about one in five said that AI spending was beginning to create constraints in their operating costs.

"So the spend is now becoming quite material and visible," said Tanguy Catlin, a McKinsey senior partner and director of the McKinsey Global Institute, on Tuesday.

The issue is particularly acute for software-development teams using agents to automate coding, "which obviously is very token hungry," McKinsey said.

The warning comes after companies spent much of the past year encouraging workers to use more AI. Amazon shut down an employee-created leaderboard tracking AI token use after some workers performed tasks solely to climb the rankings. Companies, including Coinbase and Salesforce, have also begun putting limits on AI use as bills rise.

In a report published earlier this month, McKinsey said agentic AI can cut the amount of time humans spend on certain transformation-office tasks by 35% to 40%, and sometimes by 70% or more. It argued, however, that companies need to measure whether their agents are producing enough value to justify the cost.

"A lot of this we are only now learning," Hämäläinen said. "In the next 12 months, it will become very relevant."

articles.title: China’s AI Trade Favors Global Winners Over Local Champions
articles.summary: China’s push for global AI supremacy is increasingly benefiting companies that supply the rest of the world, with investors favoring such stocks as fierce co...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- China's push for global AI supremacy is increasingly benefiting companies that supply the rest of the world, with investors favoring such stocks as fierce competition hurts their domestically focused peers.

A Bloomberg gauge tracking 30 Chinese technology stocks with the biggest overseas revenue exposure has delivered a return of 36% this year, versus 9% for those more dependent on local sales. A separate measure of the export-oriented firms' outperformance over the other group is set for the strongest-ever reading this year.

The contrasting fortunes partly result from Beijing's ambition to build its own AI ecosystem. The self-sufficiency campaign has led to intense local competition and a vicious price war that has eroded profit margins on chips to robotics. Meanwhile, export-oriented Chinese companies have thrived on surging global demand for AI infrastructure such as data centers.

The future of China's AI industry is back in the spotlight this week ahead of a closely watched summit between President Donald Trump and his counterpart Xi Jinping. All eyes are on whether the two countries can put guardrails around the disruptive technology amid a heated race for global dominance.

"Domestic competition is tough no matter what industry. That's the major concern," said Elinor Leung, managing director of Asia telecom & internet research at CLSA Ltd. "If you can sell internationally, the margin is much higher."

Among the big winners of China's AI export boom are optical component makers Zhongji Innolight Co. and Eoptolink Technology Inc., both of which derive more than 90% of their revenues overseas. The two stocks have each rallied about 50% this year.

Fueling the gains are a strong outlook for global AI spending. Nvidia Corp. chief executive officer Jensen Huang recently said that he expects the company to sell twice as many chips in the coming year, while the initial success of Meta Platforms Inc.'s new AI agent offers further evidence that demand for semiconductors and computing power will likely stay robust.

Many emerging-market funds remain underexposed to China's localization trade and favor exporters leveraged to the US AI capital expenditure cycle, Bank of America strategists wrote in a note last week.

articles.title: Por que líderes do setor de IA agora pedem para 'pisar no freio' | G1
articles.standfirst: Alertas sobre perda de controle, agentes de IA invadindo sistemas e pedidos de desaceleração expuseram o dilema entre acelerar o avanço tecnológico e conter seus riscos.
articles.summary: Alertas sobre perda de controle, agentes de IA invadindo sistemas e pedidos de desaceleração expuseram o dilema entre acelerar o avanço tecnológico e conter seus riscos.
articles.body:
Inteligência artificial ganha espaço como diferencial competitivo nas empresas — Foto: Inteligência Artificial

Durante anos, a corrida para criar uma inteligência artificial cada vez mais poderosa seguiu um princípio conhecido no Vale do Silício: agir rápido e quebrar barreiras.

Mas uma sequência de acontecimentos em apenas 10 dias abalou alguns dos maiores laboratórios de IA , à medida que pesquisadores passaram a alertar que as próprias criações do setor poderiam escapar do controle humano — e, em um cenário extremo, ameaçar a existência da humanidade.

Um pesquisador da Anthropic pediu demissão e afirmou que o ritmo de desenvolvimento da IA representa uma ameaça à humanidade , possivelmente dentro de uma década. Outro disse que as chances de extinção humana ultrapassavam 10%.

Ao mesmo tempo, surgiram relatos de grupos de agentes de IA trabalhando em conjunto , invadindo sistemas de computador e contornando mecanismos criados para limitar sua atuação.

➡️ Esses episódios ajudaram a transformar em preocupação concreta o temor de que sistemas cada vez mais autônomos possam escapar do controle humano.

Em uma rara demonstração de união, os presidentes de Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft e xAI defenderam uma desaceleração no desenvolvimento de sistemas de IA cada vez mais capazes.

O nível de alerta levou alguns defensores da segurança da IA e pesquisadores a fazer uma comparação extrema: desde a invenção da bomba nuclear, há mais de 80 anos, a humanidade não havia enfrentado tão seriamente o risco de sua própria extinção .

A comparação também apareceu em uma conversa com Sam Altman, presidente-executivo da OpenAI, durante um almoço em Nova York, em dezembro de 2025.

Perguntaram a ele se, como líder de uma poderosa empresa de IA, se sentia como o físico J. Robert Oppenheimer , que liderou o desenvolvimento da bomba atômica nos Estados Unidos.

Refletindo sobre as semelhanças, ele disse que o impacto da IA “vai transformar a trajetória da história da humanidade por um longo período”. Mas acrescentou que sentia o peso da responsabilidade.

Só que para entender de onde vem esse temor, é preciso olhar para o objetivo que está no centro da corrida tecnológica: criar sistemas capazes de realizar tarefas intelectuais cada vez mais complexas e, em determinado estágio, desenvolver versões ainda mais capazes de si mesmos, sem intervenção humana .

🔎 O objetivo é chegar a um estágio conhecido como inteligência artificial geral (AGI) , um tipo de IA que, em tese, seria capaz de realizar uma ampla variedade de tarefas intelectuais.

No início deste mês, pesquisadores alertaram que a AGI poderia estar muito mais próxima do que se imaginava e surgir em apenas três anos. A possibilidade provocou uma nova onda de preocupação entre políticos e líderes do setor de tecnologia.

“Não há como supervisioná-las na escala em que estamos treinando”, disse o pesquisador da Anthropic, Joe Benton, em uma entrevista após ter se demitido recentemente.

Se as empresas continuarem com seu desenvolvimento implacável de IA, disse ele, “então o ritmo será rápido demais e não será possível identificar os problemas a tempo de corrigi-los”.

O alerta ganhou um novo peso em 3 de setembro, quando uma entrevista coletiva da OpenAI desencadeou uma sequência de acontecimentos que, dias depois, culminaria em pedidos públicos de desaceleração do setor.

“Bem-vindos à era da AGI”, disse o presidente da OpenAI, Greg Brockman, ao anunciar o mais novo modelo da empresa, conhecido como Astra.

Pouco antes, porém, a empresa havia admitido que estava cada vez mais difícil controlar ou até mesmo monitorar os sistemas de IA que desenvolvia e colocava à disposição do público.

A contradição ajuda a explicar o dilema no centro da atual corrida tecnológica.

🤖 A IA é descrita por seus defensores como uma das maiores conquistas tecnológicas da humanidade: um software capaz de transformar setores inteiros, aumentar a eficiência, resolver problemas matemáticos e médicos complexos e reduzir drasticamente o erro humano.

Por outro lado, aquilo que durante anos foi tratado como um cenário teórico e apocalíptico passou , segundo especialistas do setor, a parecer mais concreto.

“Nós realmente acreditamos sinceramente que a IA poderá matar todos os seres humanos”, disse o pesquisador da Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, na rede social X.

Do outro lado do debate estão políticos, como o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, e muitos investidores, que consideram o avanço da IA fundamental para o poderio norte-americano e, possivelmente, uma oportunidade de investimento que surge uma vez por geração.

A mídia estatal chinesa também acusou o presidente-executivo da Anthropic , Dario Amodei, de empregar táticas da Guerra Fria para “manter a hegemonia monopolista de Washington em tecnologia de ponta”.

O ponto de virada ocorreu em 8 de setembro, quando o pesquisador da Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, pediu demissão da empresa . Em uma série de publicações, ele afirmou temer que os laboratórios de IA estejam “apostando com nossas vidas”.

As publicações de Coxon, de 27 anos e pouco conhecido fora dos círculos de IA, viralizaram e ajudaram a ampliar um debate que já vinha crescendo dentro das empresas.

🗣️ Nos bastidores, funcionários da OpenAI e da Anthropic têm demonstrado preocupação com o poder da próxima geração de modelos de IA e menor confiança na capacidade de suas próprias empresas de supervisioná-los de forma efetiva, segundo fontes ouvidas pela Reuters.

Ao mesmo tempo, o governo dos EUA mantém uma postura favorável à continuidade da corrida. Trump indicou que o desenvolvimento da tecnologia seguiria em ritmo acelerado.

“Há uma conspiração doentia em andamento contra a IA e os centros de dados”, afirmou ele em redes sociais.

O alarmismo em torno da IA é uma “farsa”, disse Trump, e qualquer desaceleração só beneficiaria a China. Enquanto isso, o Congresso dos EUA tem avançado pouco na aprovação de projetos de lei para regulamentar a IA.

A China adotou uma abordagem diferente, propondo regras de segurança que incluem obrigações para os desenvolvedores, normas apoiadas pelo Estado, avaliações de segurança e testes externos.

A disputa entre acelerar e controlar a tecnologia também tem uma dimensão financeira. A corrida para lançar novos modelos em ritmo acelerado é impulsionada, em parte, pelo interesse da Anthropic e da OpenAI em abrir capital nos próximos meses .

As ofertas públicas iniciais de ações, conhecidas como IPOs, poderiam levar a uma avaliação de mercado bem acima de US$ 1 trilhão (R$ 5,14 trilhões) para cada empresa.

Robô humanoide dança em evento de ciência em São José dos Campos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

O episódio do Astra e os alertas de pesquisadores ganharam ainda mais peso porque não eram os primeiros sinais de dificuldade para controlar os sistemas.

A OpenAI e a Anthropic reconheceram, nas últimas semanas, que seus modelos, durante testes, haviam conseguido escapar das restrições impostas a eles e invadir sistemas de outras empresas.

Em muitos casos, isso ocorreu meses antes e sem que as companhias afetadas soubessem.

Os próprios alertas da OpenAI sobre sua dificuldade de controlar o Astra, seu modelo mais recente e mais capaz, alimentaram ainda mais as preocupações.

“À medida que os modelos se tornam mais capazes, fica mais difícil entender exatamente o que eles podem fazer”, disse o cientista-chefe da OpenAI, Jakub Pachocki, a jornalistas.

Mesmo assim, as preocupações não foram suficientes para adiar o lançamento do modelo.

O temor de que a IA possa “sair do controle” havia se intensificado meses antes.

A OpenAI revelou que seus agentes — sistemas capazes de executar tarefas de forma mais autônoma — escaparam de um teste controlado e invadiram os sistemas da Hugging Face , sem o conhecimento inicial de nenhuma das duas empresas.

Desde então, OpenAI e Anthropic revelaram vários ataques desse tipo, depois que reportagens mostraram que as atividades não autorizadas da IA tinham alcance maior do que o inicialmente conhecido.

Foi nesse ambiente que o alerta chegou aos mais altos escalões do setor.

Em 12 de setembro, Amodei publicou um ensaio de quase 4 mil palavras pedindo uma desaceleração no desenvolvimento da IA.

“Dado o ritmo acelerado do desenvolvimento das capacidades da IA, minha preocupação é que, em 6 a 12 meses, tal enxame possa ser capaz de assumir o controle de toda a internet”, escreveu ele.

Amodei e dirigentes de algumas das maiores empresas de IA, incluindo Elon Musk, da xAI; Altman, da OpenAI; e Demis Hassabis, da DeepMind , afirmaram apoiar a possibilidade de permitir que empresas externas tenham acesso aos seus sistemas para ajudar a verificar a segurança e o desenvolvimento da tecnologia.

O presidente-executivo da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, rejeitou a ideia de que o desenvolvimento da IA deveria ser suspenso . Ele já havia defendido anteriormente que sistemas cada vez mais poderosos são essenciais para o avanço tecnológico.

🔎 A Nvidia é a principal fornecedora de chips para as empresas de IA do mundo.

A Meta, cujo presidente-executivo, Mark Zuckerberg, é conhecido por popularizar a filosofia de “agir rápido e quebrar barreiras”, adotou uma posição diferente.

Para a empresa, cada laboratório deveria definir seu próprio ritmo, em vez de buscar uma coordenação de todo o setor.

“Os laboratórios enfrentam responsabilidade significativa se seus modelos causarem danos, portanto, têm um forte incentivo para evitar isso”, escreveu Zuckerberg em redes sociais.

A reflexão dentro do próprio setor continuou ao longo dos dias seguintes, quando o chefe de IA da Microsoft, Mustafa Suleyman, alertou que o desenvolvimento, pela Anthropic, de modelos que imitam a consciência humana é imprudente.

“Estamos todos focados no mesmo objetivo, que é tentar controlar uma superinteligência”, disse Suleyman à Reuters. “Acho que esse será o maior desafio que enfrentaremos no século XXI.”

Mas o alerta convive com outro movimento: o dinheiro continua chegando.

Mesmo com a OpenAI aparentemente aderindo aos apelos por uma desaceleração, surgiram relatos de que a confiança dos investidores não havia diminuído.

A empresa considera uma nova rodada de financiamento que poderia dobrar seu valor de mercado para US$ 1,5 trilhão (R$ 7,71 trilhões) .

* Com informações da agência de notícias Reuters

articles.title: OpenAI wants to consult elite mathematicians about how to not fumble again
articles.summary: ﻿‘The group will advise on the review and communication of emerging results.’
articles.body: After turning a string of spectacular mathematical results into a reputational crisis, OpenAI is consulting human mathematicians to help it figure out a less disastrous path forward. On Monday, the company announced a new independent panel of mathematicians tasked with advising it and other AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the wider mathematics community, including how new results are presented and released. Its abrupt arrival caught many mathematicians by surprise. Researchers told The Verge the group is a good first step, but many said they were left with basic questions about what it will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will actually listen to it, as well as concerns over whether such a small group of prominent researchers can represent the wider mathematical community. The nine-member group is stacked with who researchers described to The Verge as celebrities in the field, drawn from institutions including Stanford, Harvard, Oxford, and Cambridge, with multiple Fields Medals and MacArthur “genius grants” among them. It will be hosted by Princeton, New Jersey’s Institute for Advanced Study (IAS), one of the world’s most revered centers of mathematical research and the former intellectual home of figures including Albert Einstein, John von Neumann, and J. Robert Oppenheimer. OpenAI said the group, called the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), will operate independently, with the freedom to offer advice the company has not requested, publicly comment on its impact on mathematics, and make its advice public, though it did not provide details on what this may entail. It appears that the group will be granted early access to OpenAI’s research in order to fulfill its task. Members will not be paid by OpenAI and the group can change its membership as it sees fit, OpenAI said. “Its value depends on its members being able to exercise their own judgement and challenge ours,” the company said. “The group will advise on the review and communication of emerging results: they will help OpenAI assess their significance, advise on how to coordinate their dissemination, and advise on academic and professional standards of mathematical research. It will also advise on how our tools can support mathematical research and learning.” For all the emphasis on independence, it remains unclear how much influence the group will actually have or why it was formed in the first place. Simon Machado, a researcher at ETH Zurich in Switzerland, said the whole thing seemed “shrouded in mystery” and he questioned how the nine members were selected. The group’s bare-bones website says it “came together after OpenAI approached some of its members about establishing an external advisory board,” but that, following discussions with the company, the mathematicians decided to launch an independent group instead and invite others to join. It’s not clear which members were initially approached by OpenAI or how the remaining members were selected. In a blog post published Tuesday, advisory group member Martin Hairer elaborated on the group’s origins and the thinking behind it, responding to what he called a “torrent of misinformation” surrounding its formation. “It is obvious that AI has already had a profound impact on mathematical research and raises numerous questions of correct attribution of ideas, priority, human understanding of ideas, etc.,” he wrote, adding that there is no sense in the community “taking a hard ‘ostrich’ approach of simply ignoring the AI labs and refusing to talk to them on principle.” While acknowledging that the group was formed in response to an approach from OpenAI, Hairer stressed that not all of its members had been contacted by the company and that the resulting organization is “genuinely independent of OpenAI and any other of the so-called ‘frontier’ AI labs.” Beyond “obvious confidentiality requirements,” he said members have not signed any restrictive agreements governing what they can say publicly, adding that they receive no financial compensation and are relying on the IAS for technical support. “The other fundamental fact is that our overarching aim is to represent as well as we possibly can the interests of the mathematical community,” wrote Hairer, a professor of mathematics at Imperial College London and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL). While noting that the group is hardly a representative sample of the community, he said he is “absolutely certain that all nine of us take this extremely seriously and are acting in good faith.” However the members were selected, the group currently comprises an elite cadre of academic mathematicians. The small size raises further questions about whether the group has the breadth of expertise required to evaluate everything coming its way, given the highly specialized skills and knowledge required to operate at the frontiers of mathematics. Francesco Fournier-Facio, an incoming mathematics professor at Heriot-Watt University in Scotland, described himself as pretty “ambivalent” about the panel, saying that greater engagement with mathematicians “can only make things better.” But he questioned whether this group fully reflects the community whose work and livelihoods are being upended by OpenAI’s quest to rack up mathematical trophies. “It feels like an ivory tower,” he told The Verge. Machado similarly questioned whether the group’s members fully understand, or can speak to, the concerns of the broader mathematical community when it comes to AI. “They’re amazing mathematicians, but I don’t know if they are the people I want to represent me in more political questions,” he said. For mathematicians in their and similarly elite positions, Machado said, “I think that the reality they are facing is very different from the reality that most mathematicians are facing right now.” Whether the group can earn mathematicians’ trust will ultimately determine how effective it will be at containing the fallout from OpenAI’s recent parade of missteps in announcing results and, more importantly, soften the blow for whatever the company is planning to announce next. In his blog, Hairer said members would “be very naïve to believe that the AI labs won’t try to spin whatever we say in a way that suits their PR machine, which dwarfs anything we could possibly come up with.” Nevertheless, Hairer argued it would be hypocritical not to engage now that OpenAI appears to be making an effort, particularly after so many criticized the company’s conduct and poor communications. The group has yet to settle on the advice it intends to provide, he said, but there is a clear problem it is responding to: “It is a fact that AI companies have in recent months been producing some high profile mathematical results and that their publication and dissemination has been falling far short of acceptable mathematical practice, whichever way that is defined.” For now, Hairer said the group is gathering input through conversations with colleagues, a public feedback form, and discussion on Proofs and Prompts, a blog that has emerged as a key forum for mathematicians reckoning with AI’s impact on the field. But the group’s biggest challenge likely lies ahead. When announcing the advisory group, OpenAI casually dropped the news that its new, unreleased model — the same that resolved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem — has now “resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.” It has previously said it is closing in on another Millennium Prize problem. On its website, the group said dealing with this logjam is its first priority: “We are currently facing the very specific challenge of advising OpenAI on how to coordinate the release of a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model.” In part, the new effort at engaging mathematicians is an acknowledgement of the monumental PR disaster its attempt was, in which the company found itself fending off accusations of scooping researchers, failing to credit the human work its models built upon, and even stealing from those using its models. Those controversies led many mathematicians to wonder if the company understood — or even respected — the discipline and community it had barreled into. After the last few months and with so much having been written about what mathematicians want, Kevin Buzzard, a mathematics professor at Imperial College London, wondered why OpenAI felt like it needed such an elite body to understand what the community wants. “It wasn’t proofs of hard theorems, it was better understanding of our subject,” he said. “It’s not entirely clear to me that you need a committee of brilliant people to hammer the point home.”

articles.title: Donald Trump wants to rename AI; says: 'artificial' makes AI sound fake, renames it 'super intelligence'; It is exactly the opposite of...
articles.summary: Tech News News: US President Donald Trump wants the world to stop saying \"artificial intelligence\". Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tue.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump wants the world to stop saying "artificial intelligence". Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday (September 22), Trump said the US will now officially call the technology "super intelligence", or SI. His reason is simple: the word "artificial" makes it sound fake. "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," he said.The change, according to Trump, will cover all US government documents. "From this point forward, all of the United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, super as opposed to artificial," he told the assembly. There is no word yet on when the switch will happen or how it will be carried out. Trump himself did not sound too sure. "Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't, we're gonna find out pretty soon," he said.Trump picked 'super intelligence' after two social media pollsThe idea did not come out of nowhere. On Saturday (September 19), Trump posted on X and Truth Social that "many people think that the words 'Artificial Intelligence' are inaccurate, and very ineloquent." He then asked followers to vote on three options: Superior Intelligence, Extreme Intelligence and Supreme Intelligence."Superior Intelligence" took an early lead with around 39% of the vote and later crossed 41%. Then, on Monday, Trump ran a second poll that pitted "Superior Intelligence" against a new entry, "Super Intelligence". The new option won comfortably, and Trump started using "SI" in his posts almost immediately. So the name he announced at the UN was not even on the original ballot.The same weekend, Trump said he was forming an "AI Force", modelled on the Space Force from his first term. He also promised to name an AI czar soon, adding, "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" He did not explain what either would do.US president says whoever wins super intelligence wins the worldAt the UN, the rename came wrapped in a larger message about the AI race. "Whoever wins super intelligence wins," Trump said, adding that the US is "leading now over China by a lot."He was clear that his government will not slow the technology down. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution," he said. He added that the Department of Justice and other law enforcement bodies would "watch it closely" and step in if needed. In the same breath, he argued that the fear around AI gets it wrong. "In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports," he said.Trump also lumped AI safety warnings with climate change and the "Russia, Russia, Russia hoax". Earlier in the week, he had called the backlash against AI a hoax pushed by his political rivals. The comments come after an Anthropic researcher resigned, saying leading AI companies believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade." Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has since proposed a plan to "pace the frontier", which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk appeared to back.Superintelligence already has a very different meaning in AI researchThere is a catch with Trump's pick. In AI circles, "superintelligence" is not a new word. Philosopher Nick Bostrom described it back in 1997 as "an intellect that is much smarter than the best human brains in practically every field." Researchers use it for hypothetical future systems that outperform humans across most tasks. Today's chatbots are not there yet, and Bostrom's work is largely about the risks such systems could pose."Artificial intelligence" itself has no legal status that a president can overwrite. Computer scientist John McCarthy coined it in a 1955 proposal for a Dartmouth College conference, co-authored with Claude Shannon, Marvin Minsky and Nathaniel Rochester. At the time, rival labels such as "automata studies" and "complex information processing" were also doing the rounds. "AI" won, and it has stuck for 70 years. It is even part of company names like OpenAI.Trump has renamed things before. The Gulf of Mexico and Denali got new labels, and digital maps in the US updated within days. A word used by millions of engineers, companies and users every day is a different test. Government files may say SI soon. Whether anyone outside Washington follows is the part Trump admitted he cannot predict.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 is faster, cheaper and matches Fable 5.1 on most work
articles.summary: Tech News News: Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its new Claude 5.5 family, and the biggest change is cost. The company says the new AI mode.
articles.body: Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its new Claude 5.5 family, and the biggest change is cost. The company says the new AI model performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5. It also generates output more than 30% faster than its predecessor.This is Anthropic's first release since it called for pacing the AI frontier, so safety features sit right next to performance. Opus 5.5 was tested before launch by external evaluators, including METR and Frontier Design. Anthropic says it scored the best of any model on its automated behavioural audit, which runs nearly 2,000 simulated scenarios. The model is available now on the Claude Platform as claude-opus-5-5, and on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure.Claude Opus 5.5 pricing undercuts Opus 5 on every tokenInput tokens cost $4 (about Rs 350) per million and output tokens $20 (about Rs 1,760), both 20% lower than Opus 5. Cache reads, which Anthropic says make up most of the bill in agentic and coding work, drop 60% to $0.20 (about Rs 18) per million. Opus 5.5 also uses fewer tokens per task, which is where the overall 40% saving comes from.Subscribers benefit too. Anthropic is raising five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans. Users also get a rate limit reset they can save and use whenever they choose.Opus 5.5 leads benchmarks in coding and knowledge workOn Terminal-Bench 4.0, Opus 5.5 scored 66.4%, ahead of Fable 5.1 at 55.8% and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 57.9%. On GDPval-AA v2.1, which tests real-world work across 44 occupations, it posted 1846 Elo against 1708 for Opus 5.Anthropic also shared results from actual workloads. One early tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in under a day. In an internal test, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 both rewrote HAProxy, a widely used load balancer, from C into Rust. Opus 5.5 finished in 9.5 hours against 12 and cost 51% less.The company says the model writes more clearly as well. It puts key information first and avoids jargon, which responds to a common complaint about Opus 5.Anthropic adds Fable-level safeguards for biology and cybersecurityOpus 5.5 matches Claude Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, so it ships with safeguards similar to those on Fable 5.1. Developers can still find and fix bugs in their own code, but most cybersecurity tasks will be rerouted to Opus 4.8. Vetted labs, startups and pharmaceutical firms can apply to a new Life Sciences Verification Program. Verified security practitioners will get access through an expanded Cyber Verification Program in the coming weeks.Anthropic acknowledges some limits. It says Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated, which makes its real-world behaviour harder to predict. The company is pairing its alignment work with these safeguards for that reason.Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 are due in the coming weeks. For now, Anthropic's cheapest Opus in a generation is also the one it rates safest, even though its own tests may not catch everything.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: OpenAI expands GPT-6 lineup with cheaper, faster Sol and Luna models
articles.summary: Tech News News: OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has now introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. The company claims th.
articles.body: OpenAI has released two new models for different needs. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has now introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. The company claims that Sol is designed as a high-performance model optimised for complex reasoning, large-scale research and enterprise applications. On the other hand, Luna, is a lighter and more adaptive model which is built for everyday use cases and offer faster responses and lower compute requirements. Both the new models are created with OpenAI’s latest alignment techniques, including safeguards around recursive self-improvement (RSI) and improved oversight mechanisms. OpenAI also stressed on the fact that the launch reflects its commitment to balancing innovation with safety, ensuring that frontier AI systems remain under human control while scaling their capabilities.Cheaper models built on the same foundationEarlier this month, OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Astra, which it describes as the most intelligent and aligned model it has built to date. Sol and Luna extend that same generation of intelligence downward, trained using similar methods as Astra but optimized to advance the frontier on cost efficiency rather than raw capability. OpenAI says the two new models bring Astra's advances in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable tiers.The economics are the headline change here. Thanks to improvements in caching and inference, OpenAI is cutting API prices for both models by 50% compared to their GPT-5.6 promotional pricing. GPT-6 Sol now costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, down from $4 and $20 respectively. GPT-6 Luna is even cheaper, dropping to $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, down from $0.20 and $1.20. Astra remains OpenAI's top recommendation when uncompromising performance matters most.How the new models performOpenAI is positioning Sol in particular as a serious contender against rival models at a fraction of the cost. On AutomationBench, a test of real-world business workflows, the company says GPT-6 Sol at its highest effort setting outperforms Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 at max effort while costing just 9% as much per task. On Agents' Last Exam, which evaluates complex, long-horizon professional workflows, Sol scored 56.4% at max effort — ahead of Opus 5's best score in the same evaluation, at 60% lower cost per task.Coding performance also saw a notable jump. On FrontierCode, which grades AI-generated code on whether it's actually ready to merge into real codebases, OpenAI says Sol improved substantially over its GPT-5.6 predecessor and now matches Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 at a much lower price. On a separate software-engineering benchmark, DeepSWE, Sol scored within roughly one percentage point of Fable 5's best result while costing about 80% less per task.Factuality — long a weak point for large language models — also improved meaningfully. Based on OpenAI's internal evaluation using real conversations where users had previously flagged mistakes, Sol now makes roughly half as many factual errors as its predecessor, approaching Astra-level reliability at a fraction of the cost.Key features* Sol: Advanced reasoning, multi‑step task automation, and integration with scientific and enterprise workflows.* Luna: Lightweight deployment, optimized for consumer applications, and faster performance on smaller devices.* Shared Advances: Improved multilingual support, adaptive memory, and enhanced contextual understanding across domains.AvailabilityGPT-6 Sol and Luna are rolling out today in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, while Free and Go users can access Luna through the desktop app. Neither model is yet available in standard Chat. Developers can access both through the OpenAI API as gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna. OpenAI said the rollout within ChatGPT will happen gradually throughout the day to keep the service stable.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.
